# Revision Sheet {.unnumbered}

(under construction...)

This page provides a concise summary of all **examinable material** for the MAS2901 exam. If a topic appears in the main notes **but is not included here**, you may assume it is **not examinable**. A dedicated section at the end lists all **non-examinable** content explicitly.

The revision sheet is organised as follows:

1. @sec-exam-details: Addresses common questions about the structure and format of the exam.
2. @sec-examinable-content-summary: Summarises all examinable material from the notes and highlights the **essential points** to focus on during revision.
3. @sec-non-examinable-content: Lists all material from the main notes that is **not** examinable.

## Exam Details {#sec-exam-details}

The exam follows the same structure and style as the specimen exam. Key points:

1. **Formula Sheet**
   * Contains **only** the distributional formulae **required for the exam**.
   * It **does not** include general results such as Fisher information, confidence interval formulae, or asymptotic approximations.

2. **Statistical Tables**
   * Standard statistical tables will be provided where necessary (e.g., Normal, Student-$t$, $\chi^2$).
   * The tables given to you in the exam can be found in <span class="xref-no-num">[Statistical Tables @sec-statistical-tables]</span>, or in the Specimen Exams on [Canvas](https://ncl.instructure.com/courses/66976/modules).

3. **Exam Structure**
   * **Section A:** Four compulsory questions worth a total of **40 marks**.
   * **Section B:** Four questions, each worth **20 marks**.  
     * You may answer **all four** questions if you wish.  
     * Only your **best three** answers will count towards your final mark.

4. **Exam notes**
   * No exam question will require writing or interpreting Python or R code.
   * When deriving **maximum likelihood estimators**, you are not required to check that your solution is a maximum unless the question explicitly instructs you to do so.
   * Clear reasoning and correct use of notation are expected; marks may be deducted for unsupported or incomplete working.

## Examinable Content Summary {#sec-examinable-content-summary}

### Part I: Foundations

<span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 1 @sec-probability-theory]</span>, <span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 2 @sec-what-is-statistics]</span>, <span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 3 @sec-types-of-inference]</span> are all **introductory material**.

The **most relevant examinable** material are the following:

#### Chapter 1 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Probability Theory @sec-probability-theory]</span>

Covers basic probability theory, mostly assumed knowledge and thus examinable (with some exceptions).

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Bayes Theorem @thm-bayes]</span> and its <span class="xref-no-num">[proof @prf-bayes]</span>: Be comfortable with using Bayes theorem for events
  $$
  \mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(B \mid A)\mathrm{Pr}(A)}{\mathrm{Pr}(B)}.
  $$
  The **proof** is unlikely to be examined.
- <span class="xref-no-num">[Random Variables @sec-random-variables]</span>: In particular, be comfortable with PDFs, PMFs and CDFs.

##### Essential Points


#### Chapter 2 - <span class="xref-no-num">[What is Statistical Inference? @sec-what-is-statistics]</span>

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- Understanding the role played by a <span class="xref-no-num">[statistical model @sec-statistical-models]</span>.
- Understanding the **difference** between data $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ and parameters $\theta$ within a statistical model.
- Understand the goal of **statistical inference** is to infer the parameter $\theta$ from data

##### Essential Points



#### Chapter 3 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Types of Inference @sec-types-of-inference]</span>

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- There are <span class="xref-no-num">[two main approaches @sec-philo-inference]</span> in statistical inference:
  1. **Frequentist Inference:** 
     - Data $X_i$ is **treated as random**
     - The parameter $\theta$ is treated as **fixed** but **unknown**.
     - Uncertainty arises from repeated experiments.
  2. **Bayesian Inference:**
     - The **data** are fixed once observed.
     - The **parameter** $\theta$ is treated as a random variable, with uncertainty described by a **prior distribution** $\pi(\theta)$.
     - Inference updates this prior in light of the data, giving a **posterior distribution** $\pi(\theta \mid \text{data})$.
- There are <span class="xref-no-num">[four types of task @sec-inference-tasks]</span> in statistical inference:
  1. **Point Estimation:**
     Give a single “best guess” $\hat{\theta}$ for the parameter.
  2. **Interval Estimation:**
     Quantify uncertainty in $\theta$ by reporting a range of values.
  3. **Hypothesis Testing:**
      Ask a **yes/no question** about the parameter $\theta$. This is done by formalising a claim (the *null hypothesis*) such as
      $$
          H_0: \theta \in \Theta_0,
      $$
      and then using the data to judge whether this claim is **compatible with the evidence**.
  4. **Prediction:**
     Use data to predict future or unobserved outcomes. **Prediction is not covered in this course**.

##### Essential Points

#### Chapter 6 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Bayesian Inference @sec-bayes-inference]</span> 

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-intro-bayes-approach]</span> the core **Bayesian** idea:
  - Unlike the frequentist approach, the parameter $\theta$ is treated as a **random variable**. 
  - The randomness captures our **uncertainty** about the value of the parameter.
- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-bayes-inference-procedure]</span> the **Bayesian** procedure:
  - **Prior:** Summarises our *prior* beliefs (before seeing any new data) about the parameter $\theta$. We write $\pi(\theta)$ to denote the **PDF** of the prior distribution.
  - **Likelihood:** We assume a statistical model, by stating $X_i \mid \theta \sim \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta)$. This induces a *likelihood* $f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)$, the **joint distribution** of observing the data $\underline{x}$ for a choice of $\theta$.
  - **Posterior:** Combines both the *prior* and *likelihood* together to summarise our **revised beliefs** about the parameter $\theta$ after observing the data. We write $\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})$ to denote the **PDF** of the posterior distribution.
- Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[prove @prf-bayes]</span> and recall <span class="xref-no-num">[Bayes theorem for densities @thm-bayes-density]</span> and understand how this yields the **posterior density**:
    $$
    \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) = \frac{\pi(\theta) \, f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x})}.
    $$
    I.e. we **condition** upon the observations $\underline{x}$ and apply @thm-bayes-density.
- In <span class="xref-no-num">[practice @imp-bayes-proportionality]</span>, we **do not need to compute** the normalisation constant $f(\underline{x})$. It is **sufficient** to know the posterior up to a constant of proportionality:
    $$
    \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) \propto \pi(\theta) \, f(\underline{x}\mid \theta).
    $$
- Be able to compute the distribution of the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})$ using the idea of <span class="xref-no-num">[conjugacy @def-conjugacy]</span>. The steps can be found <span class="xref-no-num">[here @imp-compute-posterior]</span>.

- Be able to recall and compute <span class="xref-no-num">[Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) @def-map]</span> estimators from a given posterior distribution. The steps for computing a MAP estimator are outlined <span class="xref-no-num">[here @imp-compute-map]</span>.
  - **Note:** In some cases, the MAP can be read off directly. For example, if 
    $$
    \theta \mid \underline{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(M, V),
    $$
    then the posterior is maximised at its mean, so the MAP estimator is $M$.

##### Essential Points

1. You will primarily be assessed on your ability to:
   1. **Compute posterior distributions**, substitute observed data, and interpret the resulting inference.  
   2. **Assess whether a prior distribution is consistent** with stated prior beliefs.  
   3. **Interpret and compare** Bayesian and Frequentist approaches to inference.  
   4. **Compute Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimators.**  
   5. **Obtain asymptotic posteriors** using large-sample approximations.

2. Among all posterior calculations in the course, the most **algebraically involved** is <span class="xref-no-num">[this @q-normal-normal]</span> question, where  
   $$
   X_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma), \qquad \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m, v).
   $$
   Be prepared to work through this derivation carefully.
